questions.topic: Flat index for a two-index grid
questions.learningObjective: derive the single index that names a cell when the grid is stored flat with a known width
questions.stem: A board is kept in one flat int array of width 4, so every cell has a single index instead of a row and a column. Which expression names the cell in row 2, column 1, and what is the reason?

options.text: r * width + c, because each whole row above contributes exactly width entries
r + c * width, because the row offset is added on its own before the column block
options.misconception: believes the row is a small offset and the column is the large multiplier

options.text: c * width + r, because the column selects the block and the row picks a slot
options.misconception: believes the two indices are interchangeable in the flat formula

options.text: r * width + c + 1, because a flat index is one-based like an array position
options.misconception: believes flat array indices start at one instead of zero

questions.explanation: Rows are laid out end to end, so every row above the target contributes width slots and the target row contributes the column offset, giving r * width + c. Multiplying the column instead is the tempting swap because both indices look interchangeable in the nested form, but that formula describes a column-major flattening, which stores the grid a column at a time and so puts a whole column between two cells of the same row.
questions.hint: Ask how many slots a full row of stored cells takes up before the cell you want.

questions.topic: Shape needed to rebuild a grid from a flat array

questions.stem: Eight values are held in a flat int array and must be displayed again as a two-row grid. Which piece of information does the flat array itself not carry, and so has to be supplied?

options.text: the column count, because the number of values per row is what fixes the shape
nothing at all, because eight values can only be laid out one way
options.misconception: believes the flat length alone determines the row and column counts

options.text: the index of the largest value, because the shape follows the peak entry
options.misconception: believes the largest entry records the shape of the grid

options.text: the value stored at index zero, because the first value names the width
options.misconception: believes the first stored value is a header holding the width

questions.explanation: A one-dimension array records only how many values there are, so the same eight values could have come from a two-by-four grid, a four-by-two grid, or an eight-by-one column. Either dimension has to come from outside the data, and once one is known the other follows by division. questions.topic: Index map for a quarter turn
questions.learningObjective: select the index map that performs a counter-clockwise quarter turn on a square grid
questions.stem: A square grid of side n is turned a quarter turn so that the value in the top-right corner ends up in the top-left cell. Which index map performs that turn?

options.text: new[r][c] = g[c][n - 1 - r], because the old column becomes the new row
new[r][c] = g[n - 1 - c][r], because the old row becomes the new column
options.misconception: believes the map that turns clockwise also turns counter-clockwise

options.text: new[r][c] = g[n - 1 - r][n - 1 - c], because both indices start from the far corner
options.misconception: believes a quarter turn is the same as a half turn

options.text: new[r][c] = g[r][n - 1 - c], because only the column index needs measuring back
options.misconception: confuses a quarter turn with mirroring each row left to right

questions.explanation: A quarter turn moves a cell one step along each axis: the old column index becomes the new row index, and the old row index becomes the new column counted back from the last one, so g[c][n - 1 - r] lands the old top-right corner at the new top-left. The clockwise map looks equally reasonable because it is the same two operations in the opposite order, which is exactly why the pair is easy to confuse; the other two distractors are the half turn and the left-right mirror, neither of which changes the row count.
questions.hint: Work out where the old top-right cell must be written, then invert that.

options.text: a quarter turn exchanges the counts, so new int[cols][rows] leaves room for every write
any turn leaves the counts equal, so new int[rows][rows] always has room
options.misconception: believes a turn always turns a rectangle into a square

options.text: the destination should be square so both index maps stay inside the storage
options.misconception: confuses the shape of the destination with the shape of the map

options.misconception: believes only the cell count matters and not how they are arranged

two, because two is the column count of the result matrix being filled
options.misconception: believes the innermost loop walks the result rather than both inputs

options.text: six, because the innermost loop always runs once per cell of the first matrix
options.misconception: believes the inner loop covers the whole left matrix each time

questions.hint: Find the index that means a column in one input and a row in the other.

a column of ones down the left edge and zeros in the other three columns

options.text: a single one in the last cell only, because each pass overwrites the earlier one
options.misconception: believes every pass writes the same cell of the diagonal

six: one array object for every single cell that the grid can hold
options.misconception: believes each cell of a primitive grid is a separate array

options.text: two: one array for the grid and one array that both rows share
options.misconception: believes the two rows of a nested allocation are the same array

options.text: one: a single array holding all six cells in a flattened order
options.misconception: believes a nested allocation is stored as one flat block

options.text: null, because the slots of an object grid begin as empty references
zero, because every array slot starts out holding the primitive default
options.misconception: believes an object grid reports the primitive default value

options.text: a fresh Cell with its value field set to zero, built as the read happens
options.misconception: believes reading an object cell allocates the object for you

options.text: an empty array standing in for the cell that was never assigned
options.misconception: believes a missing cell slot holds an array of length zero

six elements, one per cell, because the call walks every cell of the grid
options.misconception: believes the shallow call descends into the rows by itself

options.text: two elements, each the printed contents of one row of three numbers

questions.topic: Why a rectangular transpose needs spare storage
questions.learningObjective: explain why swapping cell pairs in place cannot transpose a grid whose counts differ
questions.stem: A square grid can be transposed by swapping cell pairs in place, but a two-row three-column grid cannot. What happens when the same swap loop is run on the wider grid?

options.text: it throws, because the loop reaches row index 2 on a grid that has only two rows
it finishes, because every pair of cells in a rectangle can be matched up
options.misconception: believes a rectangle transposes in place the way a square does

options.text: it fails to compile, because the two row arrays of a grid differ in length
options.misconception: believes rows of different lengths make the subscript fail to compile

options.text: it finishes, but the third column of both rows is quietly thrown away
options.misconception: believes the surplus column is dropped instead of being stored

questions.topic: Composing two reflections
questions.learningObjective: predict the single map produced by reflecting a grid twice
questions.stem: A grid is first reflected so that each row reads backwards, then reflected again so that the order of the rows reads backwards. Which single index map does that pair of steps produce?

options.text: a half turn, new[r][c] = g[rows - 1 - r][cols - 1 - c], both axes reversed
the original grid, because applying any flip twice returns every cell
options.misconception: believes two flips cancel out rather than composing into a turn

options.text: a transpose, new[r][c] = g[c][r], because the second flip becomes a swap
options.misconception: confuses reversing two axes with exchanging the two axes

options.text: a quarter turn, new[r][c] = g[cols - 1 - c][r], because the row count changes
options.misconception: believes reversing one axis and then the other is a quarter turn

three zeros, because only the first dimension of the allocation counts
options.misconception: believes the row count becomes the value stored in each cell

options.text: two zeros, because only the second dimension of the allocation counts
options.misconception: believes the column count becomes the value stored in each cell

options.text: three empty references, because a nested array always holds row references
options.misconception: believes a primitive grid is built out of references like an object grid

questions.topic: Column bound for a ragged grid
questions.learningObjective: choose the column count that a shared column loop over a ragged grid must use
questions.stem: Three rows of different lengths are held in a two-dimension grid, and a routine must visit every column that all three rows have in common. Which column count has to drive that loop?

options.text: the length of the shortest row, because no shorter row owns a wider column
the length of the longest row, because the loop stops at the first short row
options.misconception: believes the widest row sets the bound and the loop halts on a short row

options.text: the length of the first row, because every later row is padded out to match it
options.misconception: believes rows of a ragged grid are all padded to the first length

options.text: the row count, because the columns are counted by stepping through the rows
options.misconception: confuses the two dimensions and uses the row count as the width

questions.explanation: A column index is only meaningful for a row that owns that index, and the shortest row owns the fewest, so the shared range ends where that row ends. Taking the longest row is the tempting move because it visits more cells, but a wider row has no cell to visit in the narrower columns, so the first short row ends the run with an out-of-bounds read. questions.hint: Ask how many columns every row has, not how many the widest one has.

questions.stem: A corner cell of a two-by-two grid of integers is read with the expression grid[0][-1]. What does the running program do when it reaches that read?

options.text: it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because -1 names no column of a row
it prints 0, because the slot before the first column reads as the default value
options.misconception: believes a subscript past the end reads back a default value

options.text: it prints the last column's value, because the index wraps around to the end
options.misconception: believes a negative array index wraps to the end of the row

the record is needed because a cell value can only be read once and then is spent
